abstract: The market for rare earth elements is relatively small in value, but shortages can lead to disproportionate output losses. This column introduces a network model to quantify the output losses from a large and permanent shortage of rare earth elements. At short horizons less than one year, GDP losses range from 0.6% in the UK to 1.5% in the US and 1.8% in Japan. Supply chain risk assessments need to incorporate production networks to understand the vulnerabilities from such disruptions. Policymakers should build strategic reserves and develop domestic capacity to help withstand the short-run losses from rare earth shortages.
authors: Christian Bogmans, Maximiliano Jerez Osses, Jorge Miranda-Pinto, Jean-Marc Natal

title: Macroeconomic effects of rare earth supply disruptions

abstract: The EU's decision to phase out Russian natural gas imports raises concerns about the economic consequences of the ban, particularly its timing and uneven regional impacts. This paper examines how the wholesale gas price effects of eliminating Russian supplies depend on changing market conditions, including global LNG availability, infrastructure development and European gas demand. Using a European gas market model, we compare the impacts of an immediate phase-out under 2024 market conditions with those of a gradual phase-out under projected 2028 conditions, while distinguishing the effects of the ban from broader market developments. The results show that an immediate phase-out would lead to significant regional price increase, particularly in Central and South-Eastern Europe (4-5 €/MWh), where infrastructure constraints limit access to alternative supplies. By contrast, under projected 2028 market conditions, the ban would increase average EU wholesale gas prices by only 0.3 €/MWh and gas procurement costs by approximately 1%. Extending the phase-out to neighbouring non-EU countries would increase costs, particularly in the Western Balkans. Global market circumstances have by magnitude greater impact on absolute price levels than the Russian gas phaseout itself. The findings suggest that a coordinated phase-out of Russian gas can be achieved with limited additional wholesale market costs, provided that sufficient alternative supplies and infrastructure are available. They also highlight the importance of regional cooperation and continued supply diversification to mitigate uneven impacts across European gas markets.
title: Can Europe afford to phase out Russian gas? How timing, global supply conditions, and demand shape wholesale gas prices
